claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior in HEA nanoparticles is governed primarily by surface segregation of lower-melting-point elements.
Segregated lower-melting-point elements form a disordered surface layer.
The segregated surface layer has high atomic mobility.
The segregated surface layer reduces the effective melting temperature of the nanoparticle relative to its core.
Thermal pretreatment in an inert atmosphere can promote segregation of selected lower-melting-point elements to the nanoparticle surface.
The enriched surface layer acts as a premelted film with greater disorder and mobility than the core.
Selective elemental segregation decreases cohesive energy at the nanoparticle surface.
Decreased surface cohesive energy causes an earlier onset of surface disorder or premelting.
A disordered surface layer facilitates inward propagation of melting.
Inward melting propagation lowers the measured overall melting temperature relative to nanoparticles without surface segregation.
Nanoparticles with induced surface segregation will exhibit a diffuse, disordered surface region during heating.
Nanoparticles with induced surface segregation will have a melting onset several tens of kelvins below that of baseline nanoparticles with uniform surface composition.
Baseline nanoparticles with homogeneous surface composition have a higher onset temperature for surface premelting and overall melting than segregated nanoparticles.
The proposed segregation-controlled behavior should hold for HEA nanoparticles with diameters from 5 to 20 nm.
Surface effects dominate HEA nanoparticle melting behavior in the 5–20 nm size regime.
The proposed behavior may not apply to larger particles or bulk materials because their surface-to-volume ratio is lower.
The magnitude of melting-temperature reduction depends on elemental composition and segregation kinetics.
A comparison between homogeneous and segregation-enhanced nanoparticles using DSC, in situ TEM, and surface composition mapping can test the proposed mechanism.
